newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wholesale stocks rise in June, credit use lessens.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wholesale stocks rise in June, credit use lessens.

text.p: Stocks of unsold goods piled up on wholesalers' shelves during June at the fastest rate since the recession year 1982, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, as sales remained lackluster.

While analysts said the big rise in June inventories was surprising, it was not alarming, since there were signs that consumer spending was picking up and that much of the increase likely reflected expectations of stronger sales ahead.

Total inventories jumped 1.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted $263.93 billion in June -- the biggest monthly increase since a 2 percent rise in April 1982 and far larger than the revised 0.4 percent gain posted for May.
Previously, the department said May inventories had gained 0.2 percent.

Wholesalers' sales advanced just 0.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $210.69 billion after being revised to show no change in May instead of a 0.2 percent gain as the department previously estimated. Sales had fallen 0.8 percent in March and 0.1 percent in April.
"This inventory surge is probably temporary and much of it will be worked off in July," said economist Anthony Chan of Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio.

Chan noted that new cars and parts accounted for roughly one-quarter of the increase in June inventories. But carmakers have since reported strong per-unit July sales of new cars, which should take care of the extra cars on dealers' lots.

New-car inventories gained 5.1 percent from May to a value of $28.25 billion in June. Stocks of professional and commercial equipment and supplies grew 3.1 percent to $22.84 billion in May, the department said.

It was the sharpest pickup in auto inventories since a 5.5 percent increase in January 1991, shortly before the last recession ended in March that year. The economy has expanded steadily since that time.

In another report, the Federal Reserve said consumer instalment credit leveled off in June -- the first month in more than four years that indebtedness failed to increase -- partly because more new-car loans were paid off instead of new ones taken out.
Consumer credit was unchanged in June after rising a seasonally adjusted $2.5 billion to $1.217 trillion in May. But analysts saw it as a healthy development rather than a disturbing one.
"It's positive because it's going to reduce some of the fears about excessive debt growth," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.
"Consumers aren't pulling the plug on this expansion through less borrowing, but they are reining in its pace by curbing their spending," he added.

At the end of June, wholesalers had 1.25 months' worth of goods on hand at June's sales pace, the highest level since October last year, when they also had 1.25 months' worth. This inventories-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to sell existing inventories at current prices, was up from 1.23 months' worth in May.

Veronika White, a Philadelphia-based economist with First Union Corp. of Charlotte, N.C., said the sudden jump in stocks was not worrisome. Some of it may be related to lower ocean shipping fees from Asian production centres to U.S. ports, she suggested, as companies stepped up imports to get the benefit.

"I think most of it was voluntary," White said, adding that competitive pressures have meant reductions of 25 percent to 30 percent in shipping fees from Asian ports. Furthermore, she noted, domestic car sales were strong in July as the third quarter began.
"So on balance it would seem the consumer is back," White said. "We're certainly looking for consumer spending to pick up."
Consumers reined in spending during the second quarter after a first-quarter spree, helping to trim growth in gross domestic product to an annual rate of 2.2 percent from 4.9 percent.
Separately on Thursday, the Labour Department reported that the number of people filing for first-time unemployment benefits rose by 25,000 last week to 300,000.
But the four-week average of initial claims, which smoothes out weekly variations, fell to 303,750 last week from 325,250 the previous week -- its lowest level since the week ended Feb. 25, 1989.

"It's a very tight labour market," said Banc One's Chan, adding that the report further bolsters prospects for a pickup in third-quarter consumer spending since it means ample job opportunities and rising incomes.
